title: Open-Weight AI Models Under the EU AI Act: What Article 53 Means for Deployers in 2026
context: 2026-09-02 EAT cycle — answer-first seed covering the documentation, transparency, and compliance obligations that fall on deployers of open-weight GPAI models (Llama, Mistral, Falcon, Qwen, etc.) under Article 53 of the EU AI Act. Many deployers assume the upstream provider handles everything — the Act says otherwise. This page maps the real split of responsibilities.
body: The short answer: if you deploy an open-weight general-purpose AI model in the EU, you have obligations even if you did not train or release the model — and the scope depends on whether the model is classified as systemic-risk GPAI under Article 52b. Here is the deployer's map. First, the provider's obligations under Article 53: the entity that places a GPAI model on the EU market must (a) draw up technical documentation including training methodology, data sources, and evaluation results, (b) provide information to downstream deployers about the model's capabilities and limitations, (c) put in place a policy to respect EU copyright law, and (d) publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the training data. For open-weight models, the 'provider' is typically the foundation model developer — Meta for Llama, Mistral AI for Mistral, etc. — and they must satisfy these obligations. Second, the grey zone for deployers: Article 53 obligations technically fall on the provider, but Article 25 (value chain) makes clear that a deployer who fine-tunes, substantially modifies, or integrates a GPAI model into a high-risk system inherits provider obligations for the modified system. If you download Llama 3.2, fine-tune it on proprietary data, and deploy it as a customer-facing chatbot, you are now a provider for that fine-tuned system. Third, the practical checklist for deployers of open-weight models: (a) verify the upstream provider has published the Article 53(1)(d) training-data summary — if they have not, your deployment is not automatically non-compliant, but you lose the ability to point upstream, (b) document your own use case classification under Article 6 and Annex III, (c) if your use is high-risk, perform your own conformity assessment under Article 43 — the fact that the base model is open-weight does not exempt you, (d) maintain records of the upstream model version, provenance, and any modifications you made — Article 12 record-keeping applies, (e) for systemic-risk GPAI models (those exceeding 10^25 FLOP training compute under Article 51), verify the provider has completed the Article 55 serious-incident reporting obligations and has a compliance function under Article 53(3). Fourth, the downstream transparency trap: Article 50(1) requires that deployers of AI systems intended to interact with natural persons inform them they are interacting with AI. This applies regardless of whether the model is open-weight. Article 50(2) requires AI-generated synthetic content (audio, image, video, text constituting deepfake or synthetic output) to be marked in a machine-readable format. Open-weight models do not exempt you from these obligations. Fifth, the verified-measurement advantage: deployers using continuous measurement audit trails can demonstrate due diligence in model provenance tracking, modification logging, and transparency marking — all of which are auditable under Article 43 conformity assessment or Article 49 post-market monitoring. Bottom line: open-weight does not mean open-accountability. If you deploy it in the EU, you are in the chain of responsibility. Document your model provenance, classify your use case, and verify upstream compliance — before the AI Office verifies it for you.
